Lark Cheatsheet

Parsing toolkit for Python · pip install lark · lark-parser.readthedocs.io

1Grammar definitions

A grammar is a list of rules and terminals that together define a language. Terminals define the alphabet; rules define the structure.

rulelowercase name. A list of terminals and rules; their nesting shapes the parse tree. Recursion allowed.
TERMINALUPPERCASE name. A string, a regular expression, or a concatenation of these and other terminals. No recursion.
rule: <EBNF-EXPRESSION>
    | etc.
TERM: <EBNF-EXPRESSION>   // rules aren't allowed

Parsing begins at rule start (change with start=). Comments: // ... or # ... (since 1.1.6).

2Grammar syntax

Items & operators

a bsequence
a | balternative (may continue on the next line)
(a b)group
[a b]maybe; gives None when unmatched if maybe_placeholders=True
a?zero or one
a* / a+zero or more / one or more
a ~ nexactly n times
a ~ n..mbetween n and m times (avoid wide ranges)

Operators apply to the item on their left: a ~ 2 b ~ 3 = (a ~ 2) (b ~ 3).

Terminal literals

"string"literal string
"string"icase-insensitive string
/regex/regular expression
/regex/imsluxregex with flags (any of imslux)
"a".."z"literal range

Priorities

DECIMAL.2: INT? "." INT  // lexed before INT
expr.1: ...              // rule priority

Signed integers, default 0. Terminals: highest priority is matched first. Rules: resolve LALR collisions / Earley ambiguity.

Shaping the tree

_rulealways inlined: its children go into the parent
?ruleinlined if it has a single child (after filtering)
!rulekeeps all its terminals (none filtered)
... -> namealias: names the tree branch for this alternative
_TERMfiltered from the tree, like unnamed literals "+"

Kept in the tree: named terminals (NAME) and unnamed regexps (/[0-9]/).

Directives

%import common.NUMBER
%import common.CNAME -> NAME  // rename
%import common (INT, WORD)    // several
%import .my_file.rule_a      // relative
%ignore WS                    // skip it
%declare INDENT DEDENT        // no body
%override number: NUMBER | /0x\w+/
%extend NUMBER: /0x\w+/

%override replaces a definition everywhere, even inside imported grammars. %extend adds alternatives. %ignore is not imported.

Templates

_separated{x, sep}: x (sep x)*
num_list: "[" _separated{NUMBER, ","} "]"

3The Lark() constructor

from lark import Lark
parser = Lark(grammar, parser="lalr")
parser = Lark.open("my.lark", rel_to=__file__)
tree = parser.parse(text)       # also: start=...
parser"earley" (default): any CFG, handles ambiguity
"lalr": much faster, LALR(1) grammars only
lexer"auto" (default): contextual for LALR, dynamic for Earley · "basic" · "contextual" (LALR only) · "dynamic" / "dynamic_complete" (Earley only)
startstart rule name, or a list of names (default "start")
ambiguityEarley only. "resolve": pick one · "explicit": keep all in _ambig nodes · "forest": return the SPPF
propagate_positionsfill tree.meta with line, column, end_line, start_pos, …
maybe_placeholders[] gives None when unmatched (default True)
transformerapply a Transformer during parsing; LALR only (error with Earley). Faster, no tree built
keep_all_tokensdon't filter punctuation tokens
cachecache grammar analysis (LALR only); 2–3× faster loading
debug / strictextra warnings / raise on any potential ambiguity or collision

4Trees & tokens

Tree(data, children)a branch of the parse tree
.datarule name or alias
.childrenlist of Trees and Tokens
.metapositions (with propagate_positions)
.pretty()indented string for printing
.iter_subtrees()all subtrees, depth-first, bottom-up
.iter_subtrees_topdown()all subtrees in pretty() order
.find_data("name")subtrees whose data == "name"
.find_pred(fn)subtrees where fn(tree) is true
.find_token("TYPE")tokens of that type
.scan_values(fn)non-tree children where fn is true

Token is a str subclass with .type, .value, .line, .column, .start_pos, .end_pos.

for n in tree.find_data("number"):
    print(n.children[0])

5Transformers & visitors

Each method is named after a rule/alias (or a terminal, for transformers) and called for every matching node.

Transformerbottom-up; the return value replaces the node. Gets the children list. Call .transform(tree)
Transformer_InPlacelike Transformer, but non-recursive and edits the tree in place
Visitorbottom-up; gets the tree, return value ignored. .visit(tree), .visit_topdown(tree)
Interpretertop-down; does not visit children automatically. Call self.visit_children(tree) or self.visit(child)
@v_args(inline=True)children passed as *args. Also meta=True, tree=True. On a class or a method
return Discardremove the node from its parent (not in transformer= mode)
T1() * T2()chain transformers: T1 runs first
from lark import Transformer, Visitor, Discard
class T(Transformer):
    def pair(self, children):    # rule
        return tuple(children)
    def COMMENT(self, token):    # terminal
        return Discard
class V(Visitor):
    def pair(self, tree):
        print(tree.children)

6common.lark terminals

DIGIT / HEXDIGIT0–9 / 0–9, a–f, A–F
INT / SIGNED_INTdigits: 42 / with +/- sign
DECIMAL1.5, 1., .5
FLOAT / SIGNED_FLOAT1.5, 1e10, .5e-3 / with sign
NUMBER / SIGNED_NUMBERFLOAT or INT / with sign
ESCAPED_STRING"text" with \ escapes, incl. quotes
LETTERone ASCII letter (LCASE_/UCASE_LETTER)
WORDone or more letters
CNAMEC-style identifier: _my_var2
WSspaces, tabs, \f, \r, \n
WS_INLINEspaces and tabs only
NEWLINEone or more line breaks (CR? LF)
CR / LF\r / \n
C_COMMENT/* ... */, may span lines
SH_ / CPP_ / SQL_COMMENT# / // / -- to end of line

7Complete example: calculator

from lark import Lark, Transformer, v_args
grammar = r"""
?start: sum
?sum: product
    | sum "+" product   -> add
    | sum "-" product   -> sub
?product: atom
    | product "*" atom  -> mul
    | product "/" atom  -> div
?atom: NUMBER           -> number
     | "-" atom         -> neg
     | "(" sum ")"
%import common.NUMBER
%import common.WS_INLINE
%ignore WS_INLINE
"""
@v_args(inline=True)
class Calc(Transformer):
    from operator import add, sub, mul, neg
    from operator import truediv as div
    number = float
parser = Lark(grammar, parser="lalr")
tree = parser.parse("2 * (3 + 4)")
print(tree.pretty())             # shown below
print(Calc().transform(tree))    # 14.0
# Faster (LALR only): transform while parsing
Lark(grammar, parser="lalr",
     transformer=Calc()).parse("2*7")  # 14.0
mul
  number  2
  add
    number  3
    number  4
